meta.title: Who really said "Discretion is the better part of valour"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Shakespeare wrote it — backwards. Falstaff says “The better part of valour is discretion” in Henry IV, Part 1, first printed 1598. The proverb is older still.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Discretion is the better part of valour'?
meta.ogDescription: Falstaff’s line, reversed. Shakespeare wrote “The better part of valour is discretion” — and gave it to a knight who had just faked his own death.

answer.label: Shakespeare — but not in these words
answer.authorDates: Baptised 26 April 1564 – died 23 April 1616 · English playwright & poet
answer.sourceLine: Falstaff says it in Henry IV, Part 1, Act 5, scene 4, and it is there in the play’s first printing of 1598 ↗ — but as “The better part of valour is discretion, in the which better part I have saved my life.” The familiar reversed proverb appears nowhere in Shakespeare, and the Oxford proverb tradition traces the sentiment back to Caxton, more than a century before the play.
answer.confidenceText: Right author, wrong word order — and the idea, in quite different words, was in English print before him.

source.heading: Henry IV, Part 1, Act 5, scene 4

docMeta.dd: Act 5, scene 4 — Falstaff gets up off the battlefield at Shrewsbury
1598 first quarto, London: printed by P[eter] S[hort] for Andrew Wise
“The better part of valour is discretion” — the reverse of the modern proverb

source.excerpt: Counterfeit? I lie, I am no counterfeit. To die, is to be a counterfeit, for he is but the counterfeit of a man who hath not the life of a man: but to counterfeit dying, when a man thereby liveth, is to be no counterfeit, but the true and perfect image of life indeed. The better part of valour is discretion, in the which better part I have saved my life.
trail: c. 1477 — the idea, in different words. The Oxford proverb tradition traces the saying back past Shakespeare to Caxton’s Jason — the entry’s own locator is the Early English Text Society edition, page 23 — where the wording is nothing a modern reader would recognise: “more is worth a good retrayte than a folisshe abydinge.” The same entry also cites Euripides’ Suppliants, line 510 ↗.

1598 — the line, in print. Henry IV, Part 1 was entered in the Stationers’ Company register on 25 February 1598 and first printed in quarto later that year by Andrew Wise ↗. Falstaff’s speech is already there, in Shakespeare’s order.

1762 — the flip, in verse. Charles Churchill writes, in The Ghost, Book I: “That, even in a hero’s heart, / Discretion is the better part” — the modern word order, if not yet the modern phrase. Read it in Churchill’s collected poems ↗.

Today — the reversal, everywhere. A search of the whole canon in Project Gutenberg’s Complete Works ↗ returns “better part of valour” exactly once, in this scene, and the string “discretion is the better part” not at all.
source.excerptNote: Modern-spelling text exactly as printed in Project Gutenberg’s Complete Works ↗, which keeps the British spelling; the Folger Shakespeare edition ↗ sets the same clause as “The better part of valor is discretion” and punctuates it “I lie. I am no counterfeit.” The word order is not an editorial modernisation: the 1598 first quarto ↗ already sets the clause as “The better part of valour is discretion,” and so does every text after it.

source.rightsNote: The line was first printed in the 1598 first quarto of Henry IV, Part 1 and reprinted in the 1623 First Folio, so the text has been out of copyright for centuries in the United States and everywhere else. Only a modern editor’s notes and apparatus could carry rights — the words of the play quoted here cannot.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.kicker: The real author — of a slightly different sentence
author.heading: Who actually wrote the line
author.metaLine: Baptised 26 April 1564 – died 23 April 1616 · English playwright & poet
author.bio: Shakespeare’s date of birth is unknown; he was baptised on 26 April 1564, traditionally celebrated on the 23rd, and he died on 23 April 1616. He left some 39 plays, 154 sonnets and three long narrative poems, plus a few verses of uncertain authorship. Henry IV, Part 1 was his most reprinted play of the period — new editions in 1599, 1604, 1608, 1613, 1622, 1632, 1639 and 1692 — which is part of why one fat knight’s excuse turned into an English proverb.

misattribution.heading: Three things the quotation usually gets wrong
misattribution.intro: The credit to Shakespeare is basically sound. Almost everything else about the way this line gets repeated is not — the words, the speaker, and the claim that he thought of it.

items.who: Shakespeare, as though he wrote “Discretion is the better part of valour”
items.why: The proverb flips his sentence end to end. Falstaff’s actual words are “The better part of valour is discretion, in the which better part I have saved my life” — the reading in Folger’s edition ↗ and in the 1598 quarto alike. Search the canon and the reversed string never appears.

items.who: Shakespeare himself, quoted as his own counsel
items.why: The line belongs to a comic braggart who has just dropped to the ground on the field at Shrewsbury and played dead the moment the Earl of Douglas came at him, then risen to swear he killed Hotspur himself. In the scene ↗ it is a self-serving alibi, not authorial advice.

The Oxford proverb tradition traces the sentiment to Caxton’s Jason (c. 1477, EETS edition p. 23) — “more is worth a good retrayte than a folisshe abydinge” — and the same entry also points to a comparable line in Euripides’ Suppliants ↗. Shakespeare gave the idea its most quotable sentence; he did not originate it.

misattribution.truthLine: Shakespeare wrote the line, and the 1598 first quarto ↗ proves it — but he wrote “The better part of valour is discretion,” and he put it in the mouth of a man who had just faked his own death.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The end of the battle at Shrewsbury. Falstaff — fat, broke, and nominally fighting for the king — has traded a few blows with the Earl of Douglas and then dropped to the ground and played dead. Prince Hal, finding him there, delivers a small eulogy over him. Then, as the stage direction has it, Falstaff rises up.

The first thing he does on his feet is build a philosophy that makes lying down look brave: to counterfeit dying, when a man thereby lives, is not counterfeiting at all but “the true and perfect image of life indeed.” Shakespeare hands the definition of valour to the one man in the play with no claim on it, which is the joke. Four centuries on we quote it straight, with the word order flipped, as sound advice.
detailsBody: The saying was already old when Shakespeare reached for it. The Oxford proverb tradition tracks the sentiment to Caxton’s Jason around 1477 (EETS edition p. 23), in wording no modern reader would recognise as the same proverb; the same entry also points to a comparable line in Euripides’ Suppliants about foresight comprising bravery, offered as a parallel rather than as part of the English lineage.

The reversal was under way well before the Victorian quotation books. In 1762 Charles Churchill put it in couplet form in The Ghost, Book I — “That, even in a hero’s heart, / Discretion is the better part” — already in the modern order, if not yet the modern phrase. Churchill published Books I–III of the poem in 1762 and Book IV in 1763.

Quote Investigator has not published an investigation of this line, and Wikiquote lists it only in its ordinary sourced section for the play, with no Misattributed or Disputed entry. Nothing in the record disputes that Shakespeare wrote the sentence — the dispute is entirely over the sentence people repeat.
context.pull: Falstaff isn’t defining valour. He’s filing an excuse.
